🎓 Marketing Fundamentals · Lesson 5 of 5

Measuring What Matters & Running Simple Experiments

7 min read · Updated November 2026 · Free · Written for Kenya
Share: WhatsApp X Facebook Telegram LinkedIn

YouTube's own A/B test tool doesn't crown the thumbnail with the most clicks. It picks the one that earns the most watch time.

That one design choice tells you how the platforms think: the number that looks good isn't always the number that matters. This lesson helps you tell the difference and test ideas properly, even with a small page.

Vanity metrics vs decision metrics

A vanity metric looks impressive but doesn't tell you what to do next. A decision metric changes what you do on Monday. As investor Josh Kopelman put it, 'The real data is retention and repeat usage.'

Looks good (vanity)Better question (decision)What you'd change
Total followersHow many new followers came from this specific post?Make more of the posts that convert viewers
Total viewsAverage watch time and where people drop offFix the hook or the slow part
LikesSaves, shares and sends per 1,000 viewsDouble down on useful, shareable topics
Profile visitsLink taps, WhatsApp chats started, ordersFix your bio, link or offer
One viral postYour median views over the last 10 postsJudge progress by the typical post, not the outlier
✗ MYTH

If my follower count goes up, my business is growing.

✓ REALITY

Followers can grow while sales stay flat, for example if the audience is in the wrong city or came for entertainment, not your product. Track chats started and orders per week next to followers. If only one of them moves, you've learned something important.

Simple experiments on social

  • Change one thing at a time: the hook, the cover, the caption or the posting time. Never all four.
  • Use the built-in tools: Instagram's trial reels are shown to non-followers first, with results after about 24 hours. YouTube Studio's Test & Compare runs up to three titles and/or thumbnails on long videos.
  • Decide your rule before you start: e.g. 'run 3 pairs; the hook wins if it beats the other in at least 2 of 3.'
  • Don't stop at the first good-looking result. Checking constantly and stopping when it looks good makes lucky flukes look like winners.
💡 What most creators miss

Small numbers are mostly noise. If version A got 3 DMs and version B got 5, you haven't learned anything yet. Even YouTube's tool often reports 'performed the same' or 'inconclusive' and says that's normal. Look for big, repeated differences before you change your whole strategy.

The attribution blind spot

Much Kenyan word-of-mouth happens in WhatsApp chats and groups that analytics can't see. A sale may come from a video someone forwarded three weeks ago. So ask every buyer 'How did you hear about us?' and use a different keyword or code for each campaign.

📋 Experiment card + weekly review
EXPERIMENT
Idea: If I [CHANGE ONE THING], then [METRIC] will go up because [REASON].
Version A: [ ]  Version B: [ ]
Rule decided in advance: [e.g. B wins if it beats A in 2 of 3 tries]
Result: [ ]  Keep / Drop / Retest

WEEKLY REVIEW (Sunday, 20 minutes)
1. Chats started this week: [ ] Orders: [ ] KES in: [ ]
2. Best post by saves/shares per 1,000 views: [ ] Why?
3. Median views, last 10 posts: [ ] (up or down?)
4. 'How did you hear about us?' answers: [ ]
5. ONE thing to test next week: [ ]
✅ Do this today (under 15 minutes)
⚡ Quick check

When YouTube's Test & Compare tool picks a winning thumbnail, what does it use to decide?

YouTube picks the option with the highest watch time share, not clicks, because a thumbnail that gets clicks but disappoints viewers isn't really winning. Judge your own tests by what happens after the click too.

🧠 Key takeaways
  1. Track numbers that change your next move: watch time, shares, chats, orders.
  2. Test one change at a time, and set your winning rule before you start.
  3. Small differences are noise; look for big, repeated wins.
  4. Analytics can't see WhatsApp. Ask buyers where they found you.
